questions.prompt: Gram stain of E. coli: what is the Gram reaction and shape of these cells?
questions.explanation: E. coli: Gram-negative (pink) rods. Gram− cells lose the crystal violet–iodine complex and take up safranin.

why.A: Gram-positive cells stain purple; these are pink.

questions.prompt: Gram stain of S. epidermidis: what is the Gram reaction and arrangement of these cells?
questions.explanation: S. epidermidis: Gram-positive (purple) cocci in clusters.

why.C: These cells are spheres (cocci) in clusters.

questions.prompt: Gram stain of B. subtilis: what is the Gram reaction and shape of these cells?

why.C: This is a Gram stain, not acid-fast.

questions.prompt: This Gram stain shows a mixed species smear. What do the purple cells and the pink cells represent?
questions.explanation: Gram-positive cells stain purple; Gram-negative cells stain pink.

why.A: Reversed: Gram+ stain purple and Gram− stain pink.
why.C: Acid-fast results are pink/red vs blue.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of Gram stain reagents?
questions.explanation: Primary stain (crystal violet), mordant (iodine), decolorizer (alcohol), counterstain (safranin), rinsing between each.

why.A: Iodine (mordant) comes before the alcohol decolorizer.
why.C: Crystal violet is the primary stain; safranin is the counterstain.
why.D: The order is primary stain, mordant, decolorizer, counterstain.

questions.prompt: In the Gram stain, what is the function of iodine?

options.text: Primary stain — colors all cells purple
Decolorizer — removes stain from Gram-negative cells
Mordant — forms a large crystal violet–iodine complex

questions.explanation: Iodine is the mordant: it forms the crystal violet–iodine complex, which is large relative to crystal violet alone.

why.A: Crystal violet is the primary stain.

questions.prompt: What are the times in the lab Gram stain protocol?

options.text: Crystal violet 30 s, iodine 60 s, alcohol 10 s, safranin 30 s
Crystal violet 60 s, iodine 30 s, alcohol 30 s, safranin 10 s
Crystal violet 1 min, iodine 1 min, alcohol 1 min, safranin 1 min
Crystal violet 5 min with heat, iodine 60 s, alcohol 4 s, safranin 30 s

questions.explanation: Gram: crystal violet 30 s → rinse → iodine 60 s → rinse → alcohol 10 s → rinse → safranin 30 s → rinse → blot.

why.B: Iodine is 60 s and alcohol only 10 s.
why.C: Alcohol is only 10 seconds to avoid over-decolorizing.
why.D: Heat and 4 s acid-alcohol belong to the acid-fast stain.

questions.prompt: After the decolorizer step, what color are Gram-negative cells?
questions.explanation: Ethanol dehydrates the walls; the thick Gram+ wall traps the complex, while it escapes from the thin Gram− wall (through channels left after ethanol partly dissolves the outer membrane), leaving Gram− cells colorless until safranin.

why.B: Gram− cells lose the crystal violet–iodine complex.
why.C: They turn pink only after the safranin counterstain.
why.D: Green is malachite green in the endospore stain.

questions.prompt: Why do Gram-positive cells keep the crystal violet–iodine complex?

options.text: They have an outer membrane that blocks alcohol
Their thick peptidoglycan wall traps the large complex when dehydrated by alcohol
Their mycolic acid repels the alcohol completely
They absorb safranin more strongly than other cells

questions.explanation: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan with teichoic/lipoteichoic acids. Gram-negative: outer membrane with LPS and a thin peptidoglycan layer.

why.A: Gram-negative cells have the outer membrane.
why.C: Mycolic acid is in acid-fast cells.
why.D: Gram+ cells stay purple because they keep the crystal violet complex.

questions.prompt: A student leaves the alcohol on far too long (over-decolorizes). What will Gram-positive cells most likely look like?
questions.explanation: Be careful to avoid excess decolorization: Gram+ cells can lose the complex, pick up safranin and look pink (a false Gram-negative result).

why.A: Excess decolorizing can pull the complex out of Gram+ cells.
why.D: Green is only from malachite green.

questions.prompt: A student forgets the safranin counterstain. How will Gram-negative cells appear?
questions.explanation: Without the counterstain, decolorized Gram-negative cells stay colorless.

why.A: Pink comes from safranin, which was skipped.
why.B: Gram− cells lose crystal violet in the decolorizer.
why.C: Blue is methylene blue in the acid-fast stain.

questions.prompt: A student skips the alcohol decolorizer step. How will both Gram-positive and Gram-negative cells appear?
questions.explanation: Crystal violet colors both types purple; without the decolorizer, Gram− cells keep it and also look purple.

why.B: Without decolorizing, crystal violet stays in all cells.
why.C: The decolorizer is what separates the two types.
why.D: Crystal violet colors all cells first.

questions.prompt: What is the clinical relevance of the Gram stain?

options.text: It is a quick preliminary test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
It detects endospore-forming Bacillus and Clostridium species
It shows live, motile bacteria in an unstained wet mount
It helps choose treatment, since drugs work differently on Gram+ vs Gram− bacteria

questions.explanation: The Gram stain is the most frequently used stain in medical micro and helps determine a treatment plan.

why.C: Gram stains are heat fixed, so the cells are dead.

questions.prompt: Which smear is used for the Gram stain in Lab 9?

options.text: Slide E — a single species smear of Organism 4
Slide G — a mixed species smear of Organisms 1 and 2
Slide A — a mixed smear of Organisms 1 and 3
A negative wet mount of yeast

questions.explanation: G: Org 1 + Org 2 (Gram). A: Org 1 + Org 3 (acid-fast). E: Org 4 alone (endospore).

why.A: Slide E is for the endospore stain.
why.C: Slide A is for the acid-fast stain.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Gram-negative cell envelope is FALSE?

options.text: It has an outer membrane with LPS
It has a plasma membrane with proteins
Its cells stain pink in the Gram stain
It has a thick layer of peptidoglycan
Ethanol partially dissolves its outer membrane

questions.explanation: Gram-negative cells have a THIN peptidoglycan layer; Gram-positive cells have the thick layer.

why.A: True — the outer membrane contains LPS.
why.E: True — this lets the complex escape.
